convert_from_bitcoin.description: Work out what an amount of bitcoin is worth at Blockchain.com's current rate. Give the amount in bitcoin (0.5 rather than 50000000) and the answer comes back in the currency chosen. This is a rate lookup: nothing is bought, sold or moved.
convert_from_bitcoin.name: convert_from_bitcoin

parameters.description: The currency to quote bitcoin in. The list is the one Blockchain.com is quoting right now; refresh it if a currency you expect is missing.
parameters.name: currency

parameters.description: How much bitcoin to convert, written as bitcoin rather than satoshi. Up to eight decimal places, which is one satoshi.
parameters.name: bitcoin_amount

convert_to_bitcoin.description: Work out how much bitcoin an amount of money buys at Blockchain.com's current rate. Answers in bitcoin and in satoshi, so whichever unit the next step needs is already there. This is a rate lookup: nothing is bought, sold or moved.
convert_to_bitcoin.name: convert_to_bitcoin

parameters.description: The currency to quote bitcoin in. The list is the one Blockchain.com is quoting right now; refresh it if a currency you expect is missing.
parameters.name: currency

parameters.description: How much money to convert, in the currency above.
parameters.name: amount

get_address.description: Look up one Bitcoin address in full: what it holds, what it has received and sent in total, and its transactions newest first. Every amount comes back in bitcoin as well as satoshi, and every timestamp with a readable date beside it. Page through a long history with the offset, which the answer hands back for the next run.
get_address.name: get_address

parameters.description: The Bitcoin address to look up. Every address format works (the ones starting 1, 3, bc1q or bc1p) and a blockchain.com link to an address works too, so a value copied out of the explorer can be pasted straight in.
parameters.name: address

parameters.description: How many transactions to bring back, newest first. Raise it to see further into the history, or lower it when only the latest few matter.
parameters.name: limit

parameters.description: How many of the newest transactions to skip before the ones returned. Leave it empty for the newest. To walk through a long history, pass back the 'next_offset' the previous run reported.
parameters.name: offset

get_address_activity.description: Treat a set of addresses as one wallet. Answers with each address's own totals, the combined totals across all of them, and the transactions that touched any of them, newest first, so a wallet spread over several addresses reads as one history rather than several. An extended public key (xpub) can stand for a whole wallet here.
get_address_activity.name: get_address_activity

parameters.description: One or more Bitcoin addresses. Add a row for each. An extended public key (one starting xpub, ypub or zpub) works here too and covers every address in that wallet at once, which is the way to watch a whole wallet rather than a single address.
parameters.name: addresses

parameters.description: How many transactions to bring back, newest first. Raise it to see further into the history, or lower it when only the latest few matter.
parameters.name: limit

parameters.description: How many of the newest transactions to skip before the ones returned. Leave it empty for the newest. To walk through a long history, pass back the 'next_offset' the previous run reported.
parameters.name: offset

get_address_first_seen.description: Find the date an address first appeared on the blockchain: the timestamp of the block its first transaction was confirmed in. Useful for telling a long-standing wallet from one created this morning, which is often the first thing worth knowing about an address you did not expect. Blockchain.com asks that this part of its API is called no more than once every ten seconds, so keep it out of a tight loop over a long list.
get_address_first_seen.display_name: Get when an address was first used
get_address_first_seen.name: get_address_first_seen

parameters.description: The Bitcoin address to look up. Every address format works (the ones starting 1, 3, bc1q or bc1p) and a blockchain.com link to an address works too, so a value copied out of the explorer can be pasted straight in.
parameters.name: address

get_balances.description: Look up what one or more Bitcoin addresses hold. Answers with each address's current balance and everything it has ever received, in bitcoin as well as in satoshi, plus a combined total across all of them. An extended public key (xpub) covers a whole wallet in one row, which is the way to watch every address a wallet has ever generated. This is the cheapest way to check a balance; use 'Get an address' when the transactions matter too.
get_balances.name: get_balances

parameters.description: One or more Bitcoin addresses. Add a row for each. An extended public key (one starting xpub, ypub or zpub) works here too and covers every address in that wallet at once, which is the way to watch a whole wallet rather than a single address.
parameters.name: addresses

get_bitcoin_price.description: Get what one bitcoin is worth, averaged across the major exchanges. The chosen currency's price sits at the top of the answer ready to use, with the buy and sell sides and a 15-minute-delayed figure beside it, and every other currency Blockchain.com quotes follows underneath.
get_bitcoin_price.name: get_bitcoin_price

parameters.description: The currency to quote bitcoin in. The list is the one Blockchain.com is quoting right now; refresh it if a currency you expect is missing.
parameters.name: currency

get_block.description: Look up one block, by its height or by its hash: when it was mined, how big it is, what the miner collected in fees, and the transactions inside it. A Bitcoin block holds several thousand transactions, so they come back a page at a time rather than all at once: the answer says how many there are in total and where the next page starts. A recent block is around 8 MB at Blockchain.com's end, so give this step a few seconds.
get_block.name: get_block

parameters.description: Which block to fetch: its height (a plain number, counting from 0 for the first block in January 2009) or its 64-character hash. A blockchain.com link to a block works too.
parameters.name: block

parameters.description: How many of the block's transactions to bring back. A block commonly holds three to four thousand, so ask for what the workflow will read.
parameters.name: transaction_limit

parameters.description: Where in the block's transaction list to start. Leave it empty to start at the first, which is always the miner's own reward. Pass back the 'next_offset' from a previous run to continue.
parameters.name: transaction_offset

get_block_reward.description: Get the bitcoin a miner currently earns for finding a block. This is the subsidy, which halves roughly every four years (it was 50 BTC in 2009) and does not include the transaction fees in the block. Nothing to fill in.
get_block_reward.display_str_template: Get the current Bitcoin block reward.
get_block_reward.name: get_block_reward

get_blocks_at_height.description: List every block mined at a height, including any that lost the race. Almost always there is exactly one; to read that one, use 'Get a block' with the height, which is simpler. This action is for the rare case where two miners solved the same height at once: it names which of them ended up on the chain and which was orphaned. Transactions are left out.
get_blocks_at_height.display_name: List every block at a height
get_blocks_at_height.display_str_template: Find the Bitcoin block at height {0}.
get_blocks_at_height.name: get_blocks_at_height

parameters.description: The block number, counting from 0 for the very first block in January 2009. Bitcoin gains one roughly every ten minutes.
parameters.name: height

get_blocks_for_day.description: List every block mined on one calendar day, newest first, with its height, hash and time. Around 144 blocks are mined a day. Useful for daily reporting, and for finding the range of block heights a date covers.
get_blocks_for_day.display_name: List the blocks mined on a day
get_blocks_for_day.display_str_template: List the Bitcoin blocks mined on {0}.
get_blocks_for_day.name: get_blocks_for_day

parameters.description: The day to list, read in UTC. Bitcoin's first block was mined on 3 January 2009, so nothing earlier has blocks in it.
parameters.name: date

get_chart.description: Get the data behind any of the charts on blockchain.com as a list of dated points: the bitcoin price, the hash rate, the difficulty, the fees, how many transactions a day, how big the mempool is, and twenty-two more. Pick the series and the time range, and optionally smooth it with a rolling average. Every point carries a readable date as well as the raw timestamp, so the answer can go straight into a report.

mock_response.description: Average USD market price across major bitcoin exchanges.
mock_response.name: Market Price (USD)

get_chart.name: get_chart

parameters.description: Which series to fetch. These are the charts Blockchain.com serves through its API.
parameters.name: chart

options.label: Mining cost as a share of transaction value (%)
Transactions per day, excluding popular addresses

parameters.description: How far back to go. Long ranges are thinned to around 1,500 points so the answer stays a workable size.
parameters.name: time_range

parameters.description: Average each point over this much surrounding time, to take the noise out of a jumpy series such as the hash rate. Leave it empty for the raw numbers.
parameters.name: rolling_average

parameters.description: Begin the series on this date instead of counting back from today. Leave it empty to end at today.
parameters.name: start_date

get_latest_block.description: Get the block mined most recently: its hash, its height, when it was found and how many transactions it settled. A new one arrives roughly every ten minutes, so this is the way to tell how far the chain has moved. Feed the hash into 'Get a block' to read what is inside it. Nothing to fill in.
get_latest_block.display_str_template: Get the most recently mined Bitcoin block.
get_latest_block.name: get_latest_block

get_mining_pools.description: See which mining pools found the recent blocks and what share each one took, ordered largest first. The window is in whole days, up to the ten Blockchain.com will look back. Blocks whose miner cannot be identified are grouped as 'Unknown', which is normally the largest single entry.
get_mining_pools.display_str_template: See which pools mined the last {0} days of blocks.
get_mining_pools.name: get_mining_pools

parameters.description: How many days of blocks to count. Blockchain.com looks back at most ten.
parameters.name: days

get_network_stats.description: A snapshot of the whole Bitcoin network right now: the market price, the total mined so far, the hash rate, the mining difficulty and when it next changes, how many blocks and transactions there have been in the last day, and the average time between blocks. The figures Blockchain.com reports in awkward units (bitcoins in satoshi, hash rate in gigahashes) are repeated in the units people actually quote. Nothing to fill in.
get_network_stats.display_str_template: Get the current Bitcoin network statistics.
get_network_stats.name: get_network_stats

get_pending_transaction_count.description: Count the transactions waiting to be confirmed. One number, and the cheapest way to tell whether the Bitcoin network is congested: when the queue is deep, transactions take longer and fees run higher. Nothing to fill in.
get_pending_transaction_count.display_str_template: Count the transactions waiting to be confirmed.
get_pending_transaction_count.name: get_pending_transaction_count

get_pending_transactions.description: List the transactions broadcast to the network but not yet confirmed in a block: the mempool, newest first. Each one comes with the fee it is offering, which is what decides how soon it is mined. Use 'Count pending transactions' instead when only the depth of the queue matters.
get_pending_transactions.display_str_template: List the transactions waiting to be confirmed.
get_pending_transactions.name: get_pending_transactions

parameters.description: How many pending transactions to bring back, newest first.
parameters.name: limit

get_transaction.description: Look up one Bitcoin transaction: what it moved, what it paid in fees, where it came from and where it went, and whether it has been confirmed yet or is still waiting. Amounts come back in bitcoin as well as satoshi. The answer says outright whether it is confirmed and in which block, so a workflow can wait on a payment without reading the transaction itself.
get_transaction.name: get_transaction

parameters.description: The transaction's ID: 64 hexadecimal characters, sometimes called a TXID or transaction hash. A blockchain.com link to the transaction works too.
parameters.name: transaction_hash

get_transaction_effect.description: Given a transaction and an address, work out what the one did to the other: whether the address was paid or paid out, and how much. A transaction can have dozens of inputs and outputs, several of them the same address, so this answers the question directly instead of leaving a workflow to add them up. Answers 'received', 'sent' or 'none'. Blockchain.com asks that this part of its API is called no more than once every ten seconds, so keep it out of a tight loop over a long list.
get_transaction_effect.display_name: See what a transaction did to an address
get_transaction_effect.display_str_template: See what transaction {0} did to an address.
get_transaction_effect.name: get_transaction_effect

parameters.description: The transaction's ID: 64 hexadecimal characters, sometimes called a TXID or transaction hash. A blockchain.com link to the transaction works too.
parameters.name: transaction_hash

parameters.description: The Bitcoin address to look up. Every address format works (the ones starting 1, 3, bc1q or bc1p) and a blockchain.com link to an address works too, so a value copied out of the explorer can be pasted straight in.
parameters.name: address

get_unspent_outputs.description: List the coins these addresses can still spend (the unspent outputs, or UTXOs) with what each is worth and how many confirmations it has. Set a minimum number of confirmations to leave out anything too recent to rely on; six is the usual bar for treating a payment as settled. This is the confirmation filter Blockchain.com actually honours, which is why it is offered here and nowhere else in this integration.
get_unspent_outputs.display_str_template: List the spendable coins held by {0}.
get_unspent_outputs.name: get_unspent_outputs

parameters.description: One or more Bitcoin addresses. Add a row for each. An extended public key (one starting xpub, ypub or zpub) works here too and covers every address in that wallet at once, which is the way to watch a whole wallet rather than a single address.
parameters.name: addresses

parameters.description: How many unspent outputs to bring back. A busy wallet can have thousands; the default covers most of them.
parameters.name: limit

parameters.description: Leave out coins with fewer confirmations than this. Zero includes everything, including coins that are still unconfirmed. Six is the usual bar for treating a payment as settled.
parameters.name: min_confirmations

description: Read the Bitcoin blockchain through Blockchain.com, the explorer behind blockchain.info. Check what an address or a whole wallet holds, follow its transactions, see whether a payment has confirmed and what it moved, read blocks and the mempool, track the price in thirty currencies, and pull the data behind any of Blockchain.com's charts: the hash rate, the difficulty, the fees, the mining pool split. Free, and there is nothing to sign up for.
